newsitem.title: PERU: Aeroperu pilots reject tape theory for aircrash.
newsitem.headline: Aeroperu pilots reject tape theory for aircrash.

text.p: Pilots of Peruvian airline Aeroperu rejected on Thursday the government's theory that the crash last month of a Boeing 757, killing 70, may have been caused by adhesive tape covering height and speed sensors.

If such tapes had been placed over the sensors, the plane would have crashed immediately on takeoff from Lima rather than half an hour later over the Pacific ocean, said Cesar Betalleluz, president of Aeroperu's pilots' association.
He also questioned how the tapes had supposedly lasted a month under the sea before being discovered intact on the main body of the plane.

"It is hasty to say what happened ... This is probably a case of sabotage," he said, suggesting that third parties may have placed the tape on the wreckage during rescue operations in order to establish a false cause.

The investigation into the Oct. 2 crash took a controversial twist on Wednesday when Peru's transport ministry pointed at adhesive tapes left on the plane by maintenance workers as the possible cause.
The obstruction of these instruments "could explain the erroneous and confused information about height and speed that was received by the pilots after takeoff," the ministry said.

Previously, the Peruvian government had pinned the blame for the accident on technical faults which made the computers aboard the plane "go crazy," leaving pilot, Eric Schreiber, without instruments as he struggled to return to Lima.

An official investigating team from Aeroperu, Boeing Co., engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the U.S. National Transporation Safety Board, has so far reserved judgment on the causes of the crash.
Rescue workers had by the weekend found the corpses of 55 victims from the crash and continued this week to look for the remaining 15, according to Aeroperu.
The 70 dead came from Chile, Peru, Mexico, Ecuador, the United States, Italy, Britain, New Zealand, Spain, Colombia and Venezuela.
